chapter.name: The State, the Government, and You

questions.q: In the chapter's comparison of a school with a state, what does the school stand for?
questions.a: The school stands for the state, which remains while the principal and teachers, who stand for the government, come and go.
o: The state, which stays while the teachers come and go
The government, which changes when a new principal comes
Sovereignty, the power to run its own affairs without outside control
The people, since a school is made up of its students

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four important parts of a state as given in the chapter?
questions.a: The four parts are people, land, government and sovereignty. A written constitution is discussed elsewhere in the chapter but is not one of the four parts.
o: A written constitution
People who live in the country
A fixed area or territory
A system to run the country

questions.q: A news report says, 'No other country or outside body can interfere in the internal affairs of this nation.' Which part of the state does this sentence describe?
questions.a: Sovereignty is complete control over one's own matters and the ability to make and implement laws for one's own needs, so no outside body can interfere.
o: Sovereignty
A defined territory
A permanent population
A government

questions.q: Two neighbouring states mark their common border with stone pillars across an open field where there is no river, hill or road to follow. Arjun argues, 'This cannot be a real boundary, because boundaries must be drawn by nature.' Which idea from the chapter answers him?
questions.a: The chapter says boundaries are not necessarily geographical features but lines agreed upon by the neighbouring states, so pillars across a field can be a proper boundary.
o: Boundaries are lines agreed upon by neighbouring states and need not be natural features
A territory counts as defined only when a river or a mountain bounds it, so Arjun is right
Boundaries are fixed by the government of the larger state and accepted by the smaller one
Boundaries are fixed by the people of the border villages without the neighbouring state

questions.q: In Roshini didi's talk with Rahul, he asks why a state needs a government at all. Which answer follows the chapter's reasoning?
questions.a: Because people live together, laws have to be made and implemented for the state to function, and that is what the government does.
o: People living together need laws made and run, which the government does
A government is needed to attract a permanent population to the land
A government is needed to keep tourists and outsiders out of the territory
A government is what gives the state its fixed area and its boundaries

questions.q:
Read the following statements.
1. The government makes laws, enforces laws and resolves disputes.
2. A state comes to an end whenever its government changes after an election.
3. Sovereignty means no outside body can interfere in the internal affairs of the state.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the government can change after elections but the state remains the same, like a school whose teachers come and go.
o: 1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A group of tourists staying in a town for a week cannot be counted as its permanent population.
Reason (R): A government makes laws, enforces laws and resolves disputes.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Tourists are left out because they do not live together or identify with the place; what a government does is a different point.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each part of a state in Column A with what the chapter says it is, in Column B.
Column A: 1. People  2. Land  3. Government  4. Sovereignty
Column B: a. a system to run the country  b. the full power to make laws and take decisions without any outside control  c. the citizens who live in the country  d. a fixed area or territory
questions.a: People are the citizens who live in the country, land is a fixed area, government is a system to run the country, sovereignty is full power without outside control. The wrong pairings swap people with land or government with sovereignty.

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter say a permanent population has that tourists, who just visit and move on, do not? (b) Lakhs of pilgrims visit a temple town for a fortnight every year. Do they form the permanent population of that town? Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) They identify with the place, have something common and shared, and live together. (b) No. Like tourists they visit and move on, so they have no identification with the place and do not live together there.
s: Part (a): identification with the place, shared things, living together
Part (b): No, they only visit and move on, as tourists do

questions.q: (a) Name the four features of a state as the chapter's summary lists them. (b) A newspaper writes, 'The State has announced free bus passes for girls.' Which feature is the writer really pointing to, and why is the word 'state' used for it?
questions.a: (a) Defined territory, permanent population, a government and sovereignty. (b) The government. It acts on behalf of the state and is the face of the state that we see in action every day.
s: Part (a): territory, population, government, sovereignty
Part (b): the government, which acts for the state and is the face we meet daily

questions.q: Define sovereignty and give one reason the chapter gives for calling it essential to a state.
questions.a: Sovereignty is the full power to make laws and take decisions without any outside control. It is essential because the state must have complete control over its own matters and make laws according to its own needs, with no other state interfering.
s: Defines sovereignty as full power to make laws and decisions without outside control
Gives the reason: laws suited to its own needs, no interference in internal affairs

questions.q: What is meant by a 'geographically defined territory'? Who agrees on its boundaries?
questions.a: It is a place or area with clear boundaries. The boundaries are not necessarily natural features but lines agreed upon by the neighbouring states.
s: A place or area with clear boundaries
Boundaries are lines agreed upon by the neighbouring states

questions.q: The chapter says people often use 'state' and 'government' as if they meant the same. Give the two reasons it lists for this mix-up.
questions.a: The government runs the daily work of the state, and we usually deal with the government and not with the whole state.
s: Reason 1: the government runs the daily work of the state
Reason 2: we usually interact with the government, not the whole state

questions.q: Imran says, 'When a new government is formed, a new state is formed too, just as a new principal makes a new school.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The government can change after elections but the state remains the same. The chapter's own comparison shows this: a school stays although principals and teachers come and go, so Imran's comparison supports the opposite of what he says.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Reason: the government changes after elections but the state remains
Uses the school comparison, where the school stays as teachers come and go

questions.q: A quiz team says: 'Zorbia has 40 lakh people whose families have lived there for generations, a border agreed with its neighbours and an elected council that runs it. But every law it makes must be approved by a neighbouring country before it takes effect. So Zorbia is a state.' Show, using the chapter, that this claim cannot be right.
questions.a: Zorbia has people, land and a government, but not sovereignty. Sovereignty is the full power to make laws without any outside control, and Zorbia's laws need outside approval, so another country interferes in its affairs. A state needs all four features.
s: Names the features Zorbia does have: people, land, government
Identifies sovereignty as the missing feature
Explains that outside approval of laws is outside control, so Zorbia cannot be a state

questions.q: Write a short conversation of three or four lines in which a student wrongly uses 'state' and 'government' as if they were the same. Then correct her, using the school comparison from the chapter.
questions.a: Any sensible conversation, e.g. 'The state changed after the election.' Correction: only the government changed; the state stays, just as a school stays when the principal and teachers change.
s: A realistic conversation with the mix-up
Identifies which word is wrongly used
Corrects with the school comparison: state remains, government can change

questions.q: 'The population and the territory are clear parts of the state, yet the government is a part of the state and not the state itself.' Explain this statement using the chapter's reasoning.
questions.a: People who identify with a place and live there form a permanent population that develops its own culture and society. The territory is a place with boundaries agreed upon with neighbours. Because people live together, laws must be made and implemented, which is what the government, made of leaders, ministers and officials, does. But it is only one part, and it can change after elections while the state remains, like teachers coming and going while the school stays.
s: Permanent population: identifies with and lives in a place, develops its own culture and society
Territory with boundaries agreed upon by neighbouring states
People living together need laws made and implemented, so the government exists
Government is made of leaders, ministers and officials who make laws, enforce them and resolve disputes
Government is only one part and can change while the state remains, with the school comparison

questions.q: A state needs all four of its parts. For each situation below, name the part that is missing and say what goes wrong: (i) every resident is a short-term visitor; (ii) the area has no boundaries that its neighbours accept; (iii) nobody makes or enforces laws; (iv) an outside body decides the state's laws. Then say what this shows.
questions.a: (i) Permanent population is missing: visitors share nothing and do not live together. (ii) A defined territory is missing: boundaries are lines agreed upon by neighbouring states. (iii) Government is missing: no one makes laws, enforces them or resolves disputes. (iv) Sovereignty is missing: outside control interferes with the state's own matters. It shows that a state is complete only with all four.
s: (i) Population missing, with reason
(ii) Defined territory missing, with reason
(iii) Government missing, with reason
(iv) Sovereignty missing, with reason
Concludes that all four are needed together

questions.q:
Class 7 of a school in Pune builds a model country called Sundara as a term project. Its 300 citizens are the students of the class, who stay in the model for the whole term. A taped map on the hall floor shows Sundara's area, and its lines were fixed after talks with the neighbouring class's model country, Taranga. A cabinet of five students makes the rules, carries them out and settles quarrels. The class teacher, however, has to approve every rule before it can take effect. After a mid-term election a new cabinet takes over, while the citizens and the floor map stay the same. The teacher announces, 'Sundara is now a complete state.'
(a) Which part of a state does the cabinet stand for, and what does the mid-term election show about it?
(b) Would the 300 students count as Sundara's permanent population if they came only for one afternoon? Explain using the chapter.
(c) Which feature of a state is Sundara missing, and why?
(d) Is the teacher's announcement correct? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) The government; it can change after an election while the citizens and territory (the state) stay. (b) No. A state has a permanent population; students who stay all term fit this, visitors for an afternoon would not. (c) Sovereignty, because an outside authority, the teacher, controls its rules. (d) No. Sundara has population, territory (agreed lines) and a government, but without sovereignty it is not a complete state; it would become one only if the cabinet had the final say.
s: Part (a): government, which can change after elections while the state remains
Part (b): a state needs a permanent population; an afternoon's visitors would not be one
Part (c): sovereignty is missing because an outside authority approves every rule
Part (d): says No, using the missing sovereignty

questions.q:
At a quiz in a Jaipur school, the quiz-master reads four statements and asks each team to mark them 'state' or 'government'.
S1: 'It decided to open twenty more anganwadi centres this month.'
S2: 'It has stayed the same although three different parties have formed ministries over twenty years.'
S3: 'It has crores of citizens, a fixed area, and complete freedom from outside control, besides those who run its administration.'
S4: 'It is a group of leaders, ministers and officials who enforce laws and settle disputes.'
Team Aravalli answers S1 'state', S2 'state', S3 'state' and S4 'government', and claims a mark for S1 because 'the state did this' is how people talk.
(a) Which statements describe the government and which the state?
(b) What does S2 show about what happens to each after elections?
(c) Why do people say 'the state did this' in daily life?
(d) Should the quiz-master give Team Aravalli the mark for S1? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) S1 and S4 describe the government; S2 and S3 describe the state. (b) The government changes with different parties, while the state remains the same. (c) The government acts on behalf of the state and is the face we see in action every day, so people use the words loosely in daily speech. (d) No. S1 describes an action of the government, so in a quiz on the difference between the two, 'state' is wrong for S1; the everyday-speech point in (c) explains the habit but does not earn the mark.
s: Part (a): S1 and S4 government, S2 and S3 state
Part (b): government changes, state remains
Part (c): government acts for the state and is its daily face
Part (d): No mark, because S1 is a government action

questions.q: According to the chapter, the police in India are responsible for maintaining law and order within which unit?
questions.a: The chapter says the police maintain law and order within each state and are part of the state government.
o: Each state
The whole country as a single force
Each court of law
Each village panchayat only

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a task of the police as described in the chapter?
questions.a: Making laws belongs to the legislature. The police enforce the law, maintain peace, protect citizens, investigate and present cases to the judiciary, and run awareness programmes.
o: Making the laws that the police later enforce
Investigating a case and presenting it to the judiciary
Running a road safety awareness programme
Maintaining peace and protecting citizens

questions.q: In the chapter's picture of how people, police and the organs of government interact, what is the police's role towards the judiciary?
questions.a: The police investigate cases and present them to the judiciary. Deciding cases belongs to the courts, protecting rights to the Constitution and laws, and electing leaders to the people.
o: To investigate cases and present them to the judiciary
To decide cases and punish those found guilty
To protect rights through the Constitution and laws
To elect the leaders who will make the laws

questions.q: The government departments whose names we see on boards near our homes belong to which part of the government?
questions.a: Departments implement the policies and laws made by the legislature, which makes them part of the executive.
o: The executive
The legislature
The judiciary
Civil society

questions.q: A police station in a Nashik locality holds a talk at a school on women's safety and an awareness walk against drug abuse. Ritu says, 'This is not police work; the police only catch criminals.' Which point from the chapter answers her?
questions.a: The chapter says that beyond crime control the police contribute to social change by promoting safety, justice and a better quality of life, for example through awareness programmes.
o: Beyond crime control, the police promote safety through awareness work
Awareness work belongs to the judiciary, and the police only lend a helping hand
Awareness programmes are run by the police only when a court orders them to
Only the Central Government can run awareness programmes of this kind

questions.q: During a festival procession in Pune, a police inspector uses force to stop a fight, but also lets an ambulance through the crowd and does not stop anyone from walking home peacefully. Which statement from the chapter does this show?
questions.a: The chapter says the police can legally use force for safety but must respect and protect the rights guaranteed under the Constitution.
o: The police may use force legally but must respect constitutional rights
The police may use any force they find useful because they are agents of the state
The police must avoid force completely because the Constitution forbids it
The police may restrict rights in a crowd because rights apply only at home

questions.q:
Read the following statements.
1. The police in India are part of the state government.
2. Government departments carry out the policies and laws made by the legislature.
3. In our daily lives we mainly interact with departments of the executive.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are given in the chapter: the police are part of the state government, departments implement the legislature's laws, and we mainly meet the executive in daily life.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The police must respect the fundamental rights of citizens even while enforcing the law.
Reason (R): The Constitution guarantees rights and limits the power of government, so force cannot be used unchecked.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and the reason explains the assertion: because the Constitution guarantees rights and limits government's power, the police cannot use their power unchecked.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name two awareness programmes the chapter lists as part of police work. (b) Why does the chapter say that such programmes show the police contribute to 'social change'?
questions.a: (a) Any two of road safety, drug abuse, women's safety. (b) Because beyond controlling crime they promote safety, justice and a better quality of life.
s: Part (a): two of road safety, drug abuse, women's safety
Part (b): beyond crime control they promote safety, justice and quality of life

questions.q: (a) The police are called 'agents of the state'. Which power do they legally hold that ordinary citizens do not? (b) What limits this power, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) The legal use of force to keep people safe and secure, free from crime and violence. (b) The Constitution: the police must respect and protect the rights it guarantees.
s: Part (a): the legal use of force for safety
Part (b): the Constitution and the rights it guarantees limit the power

questions.q: Differentiate between the work of the police and the work of the courts using the chapter's picture of how people, police and organs of government interact.
questions.a: The police enforce the law, maintain peace, protect citizens and investigate and present cases to the judiciary. The courts, with the Constitution and laws, protect people's rights and ensure justice.
s: Police: enforce law, keep peace, investigate and present cases
Courts: protect rights and ensure justice under the Constitution and laws

questions.q: What are government departments, which function of government do they form part of, and what do they do with the legislature's laws?
questions.a: They are the offices whose names we see on boards, part of the executive. They implement the policies and laws made by the legislature.
s: Departments are part of the executive
They implement policies and laws made by the legislature

questions.q: Name the three pillars of government and say which one we meet most in our daily lives. Give one reason.
questions.a: Legislature, executive and judiciary. We meet the executive most because its departments implement policies and laws in places we use every day.
s: Names legislature, executive and judiciary
Executive, with its departments, is the one met in daily life

questions.q: Karan says, 'Since the police can use force, nobody can question what they do.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The police may use force legally only to keep people safe and must respect and protect constitutional rights. The Constitution limits the government's powers because unchecked power would threaten citizens' rights, and courts protect those rights.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Police must respect rights guaranteed by the Constitution
Constitution limits power, since unchecked use of power would threaten rights

questions.q: Write a four-line situation in which a police officer's action keeps the public safe and also respects a citizen's right. Mark the two ideas in your story.
questions.a: Any suitable situation, e.g. an officer stops a quarrel at a bus stand using necessary force and later lets the quarrelling person speak to a lawyer. Safety is the legal use of force; respect is protecting the person's constitutional rights.
s: A realistic four-line situation
Shows the police keeping people safe
Shows respect for a right guaranteed by the Constitution

questions.q: Explain how people, the police and the courts are linked in the chapter's picture of governance.
questions.a: People elect leaders to represent them. The police enforce the law, maintain peace, protect citizens and investigate and present cases to the judiciary. The Constitution, laws and courts protect people's rights and ensure justice.
s: People elect leaders to represent them
Police enforce law and present cases to the judiciary
Constitution, laws and courts protect rights and ensure justice

questions.q: Describe the role of the police in a state beyond controlling crime, and explain why they must respect rights while using force.
questions.a: The police are part of the state government and work with local communities in towns, cities and villages. They are agents of the state who can legally use force for safety, work with courts and prisons, and run awareness programmes such as road safety and drug abuse. But the Constitution limits government power: if it did not, officers might use power unchecked and threaten citizens' rights.
s: Part of the state government working with local communities
Legal use of force for a safe and secure environment
Works with courts and prisons
Awareness programmes beyond crime control
Must respect rights because the Constitution limits power and unchecked power would threaten rights

questions.q: 'The three pillars of government work together, but in daily life we meet mostly one of them.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: The three pillars are the legislature, which makes laws, the executive, which implements them through departments, and the judiciary, which ensures that laws are followed. Together they form the key pillars of government. In daily life we mainly meet departments on boards near our homes, which belong to the executive, so one pillar is the one we meet, though it works within the laws made and checked by the others.
s: Names the three pillars
Legislature makes the laws
Executive departments implement policies and laws
Judiciary ensures the laws are followed
Explains that daily life mostly meets the executive's departments

questions.q:
The Sector 9 police station in a town has 600 working hours a month. It spends 360 hours on thefts and other cases, which it prepares for presentation, 150 hours patrolling to keep the peace, and 90 hours on talks in schools about road safety and drug abuse. With 40 thefts pending, a senior officer suggests dropping the school talks altogether and using all 90 hours on case work.
(a) To which organ of government does the station present the cases it prepares?
(b) Which of the three activities goes beyond crime control, and what percent of the 600 hours does it take?
(c) Why does the chapter count it as part of the police's work and not as a favour?
(d) Should the suggestion be accepted? Decide and justify using the chapter and your figure.
questions.a: (a) The judiciary. (b) The school talks (awareness programmes); 90 of 600 hours is 15 percent. (c) Beyond crime control, the police promote safety, justice and a better quality of life through awareness programmes. (d) No. Dropping them removes a role the chapter assigns to the police; the 15 percent is small enough that a smaller shift, not removal, can help the pending thefts. A creditable answer must use the chapter's role and the 15 percent, not a bare opinion.
s: Part (a): the judiciary
Part (b): the school talks, 15 percent
Part (c): police promote safety, justice and quality of life beyond crime control
Part (d): No, justified with the chapter's role and the 15 percent figure

questions.q:
In Kalyan town the state legislature passes a law that every government school must have a safe approach road. The Public Works Department builds one to the Girls' High School. A landowner then fences off part of the new road. The headmistress says, 'Only the court can act here. The police deal only with thefts, so there is no point going to them.'
(a) Which organ of government made the law, and to which organ does the Public Works Department belong?
(b) Name two things the police do according to the chapter.
(c) Which organ protects the girls' rights and ensures justice in the end?
(d) Is the headmistress right that the police have no part in this? Decide and justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The legislature made the law and the department belongs to the executive. (b) Any two of: enforce the law, maintain peace, protect citizens, investigate crimes and present the case to the judiciary. (c) The judiciary, through the Constitution, laws and courts. (d) No. The police enforce the law and maintain peace and can investigate the fencing and present the case to the judiciary; the court is the final protector of rights, but the police are the first step in enforcing the law.
s: Part (a): legislature made it, executive department built it
Part (b): two police roles from the chapter
Part (c): the judiciary protects rights and ensures justice
Part (d): No, because police enforce the law and present cases to the judiciary

questions.q: Which of the following gives the core idea of a democracy as explained in the chapter?
questions.a: Democracy is rule by the people, who choose their government through free and fair elections. Elected head of state and limits on rulers describe a republic.
o: Rule by the people, who choose their government through free and fair elections
Rule by an elected head of state whose power is limited by a constitution
Rule by a family whose head inherits power but follows the laws
Rule by officers who are selected through examinations

questions.q: Which of the following statements about a republic is NOT correct?
questions.a: A republic's head of state may be elected directly or indirectly, as India's president is elected by a group of elected representatives. So it is wrong to say direct election by all voters is required.
o: Its head of state must be elected directly by all the voters
Its head of state is elected, directly or indirectly, by the people
The powers of its head of state are limited by a constitution or laws
Its head of state is not a king or queen who inherits power

questions.q: In 1782 an officer suggested to General George Washington that he should become king of America. What did Washington do?
questions.a: He firmly refused, saying such a plan would harm the country and that he believed only in a government by the people under a constitution.
o: He firmly refused, saying it would harm the country
He accepted and became the first President
He accepted on condition that he would rule with a council
He asked the British king to decide whether he should accept

questions.q: A student council votes by a large majority that no food from outside may be carried on school trips. Sneha, who has diabetes and must carry her own meals, is left out of the discussion. Which idea from the chapter does this situation test?
questions.a: Dominance of the majority means pursuing the interests of the majority alone, to the harm of the rights of minorities. The chapter says a republic defends against it by protecting the voice of the minority.
o: Protecting a minority's rights against the dominance of the majority
Electing the head of state by a group of elected representatives
Choosing the government through free and fair elections only
Replacing a hereditary king with a person chosen by vote

questions.q: A country has a queen as head of state, and her position passes to her eldest child. Its people freely elect their parliament, and the government is answerable to it. Which description fits this country?
questions.a: A country that elects its government freely is a democracy; with a hereditary monarch as head of state it is not a republic, like the UK, Canada and Sweden in the chapter.
o: A democracy but not a republic
A republic but not a democracy
Both a democracy and a republic
Neither a democracy nor a republic

questions.q:
Read the following statements.
1. India's president is elected directly by all the voters of the country.
2. A country can be both a democracy and a republic, as India and the U.S.A. are.
3. In a republic the powers of the head of state are limited through a constitution or laws.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false: the president is elected not directly by the people but by a group of elected representatives.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A country that holds free and fair elections is always a republic.
Reason (R): The UK, Canada and Sweden are democracies that each have a monarch.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The assertion is false and the reason is true. The UK, Canada and Sweden hold free elections but have monarchs, so they are democracies and not republics.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with its meaning or example in Column B.
Column A: 1. Democracy  2. Republic  3. Dominance of the majority  4. Dongria Kondh sacred hills
Column B: a. interests of the majority alone are pursued, harming minorities  b. head of state is elected and not hereditary  c. rule by the people through free and fair elections  d. mining not allowed because the community opposed it and the law protected its rights
questions.a: Democracy is rule by the people; a republic has an elected head of state; dominance of the majority harms minorities; the sacred hills example shows a community's rights protected by law. Wrong pairings swap democracy with republic or the definition with the example.

questions.q: (a) What do 'demos' and 'kratos' mean? (b) How does a democracy put this meaning into practice when it chooses its government?
questions.a: (a) Demos means people and kratos means rule, so democracy is rule by the people. (b) People have the power to choose their government through free and fair elections.
s: Part (a): demos = people, kratos = rule
Part (b): choosing the government through free and fair elections

questions.q: (a) Who elects the President of India? (b) Does this make India any less of a republic? Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) A group of elected representatives, and not directly by the people. (b) No. In a republic the head of state may be elected directly or indirectly by the people, and what matters is that the head is not a king or queen who inherits power.
s: Part (a): a group of elected representatives, not directly by people
Part (b): no, because indirect election still makes the head of state elected and not hereditary

questions.q: (a) State one way in which India and the UK are alike in their government. (b) State the difference between them in the head of state.
questions.a: (a) In both the people elect their representatives and the government is accountable to parliament. (b) The UK has a monarch as head of state, while India's president is elected.
s: Part (a): both elect representatives and the government answers to parliament
Part (b): UK has a monarch, India has an elected president

questions.q: What is meant by 'dominance of the majority'? Name one example from the chapter in which a minority's rights were protected.
questions.a: It is a situation where only the interests of the majority are pursued, harming the rights of minorities. Examples: the RWA changed its late-night delivery rule to exclude food and medicines, or the Dongria Kondh's sacred hills were protected from mining.
s: Defines dominance of the majority
Names a correct example from the chapter

questions.q: The chapter retells Kautilya's picture of 'big fish eating the smaller fish'. What does it warn about, and what does Kautilya say the king must follow?
questions.a: It warns that without government, law and order, society becomes chaotic and the powerful harm the weak. The king must follow Raja Dharma and have a good governance system.
s: Warning: without law and order the powerful eat the weaker
The king must follow Raja Dharma and ensure good governance

questions.q: Tara says, 'In a republic the elected head of state can make any law she likes, because the people elected her and a republic is only about elections.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. In a republic the head of state is elected and not hereditary, but her power is limited by a constitution or laws. The chapter's example is Washington, who refused to be king because he believed only in government by the people under a constitution. In India the Constitution guarantees fundamental rights and limits those in power.

A republic's rulers are limited by a constitution or laws
Supports with Washington or India's Constitution and rights

questions.q: Make up a rule that a school's student council could pass by majority vote but that would hurt a minority of students. Then change it as the RWA changed its rule, and name the chapter idea you have used.
questions.a: Any sensible rule, e.g. no lunch to be eaten in class, harming a student who must eat on medicine time; change it to exempt such students. The idea is protection of a minority against dominance of the majority.

Names protection against dominance of the majority

questions.q: How does the Dongria Kondh example show that the law protects a community's rights in India? Answer in three points.

questions.q: Compare a democracy and a republic and explain how India is both.
questions.a: A democracy is rule by the people, who choose the government in free and fair elections. A republic has a head of state who is elected, directly or indirectly, and not hereditary, and whose power is limited by a constitution or laws. A country can be both, like India or the U.S.A., but the UK, Canada and Sweden are democracies and not republics. India's people elect representatives, and the president is elected by a group of elected representatives, unlike the British monarch, so India is a democracy and a republic.

Defines republic including limits by a constitution or laws

Democracies that are not republics, with an example

questions.q: 'In a republic the rule of law is more powerful than the wishes of the majority.' Justify this using the RWA example and the protection given by the Constitution.
questions.a: The RWA banned deliveries after 9 pm by a majority vote, ignoring a minority. When an elderly resident collapsed because her medicine could not be delivered, the rule was changed to exclude food and medicines, protecting the voice of the minority. Dominance of the majority harms minorities' rights. In a republic like India, France or the USA the Constitution stops elected leaders from passing laws that go against basic rights such as freedom of speech, religion or equality before the law.

questions.q:
The library committee of a school in Nagpur has 80 student members. By 56 votes to 24 they decide that the library will close at 1 pm every day. The 24 who voted against include students who can use the library only after their bus arrives at 2 pm. The majority says, 'We won the vote, so the rule is fair and nothing needs changing.'
(a) Which problem named in the chapter does the majority's argument ignore?
(b) What percent of the members voted against, and what does a republic protect such a group from?
(c) What in India's system stops elected representatives from passing laws that violate basic rights?
(d) Is the majority's claim that the rule is fair simply because it won the vote correct? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Dominance of the majority. (b) 24 of 80 is 30 percent; a republic protects the rights of smaller groups from an unfairly powerful majority. (c) The Constitution, which guarantees fundamental rights and limits power. (d) No. Winning a vote does not make a rule fair when it ignores the needs of a minority; the committee should relax the rule, for example by keeping the library open for the 2 pm students, because the chapter wants minority rights protected.
s: Part (a): dominance of the majority
Part (b): 30 percent; a republic protects smaller groups from an unfairly powerful majority
Part (c): the Constitution with fundamental rights
Part (d): No, because winning a vote does not protect the minority

questions.q:
A debate club in Lucknow prepares for the motion 'A powerful ruler is better than a constitution'. Its research team brings two stories. Story 1: in 1782, as the American War of Independence was ending, an officer wrote to General George Washington suggesting he should become king of America. Story 2: Kautilya, author of the Arthashastra, compares a society without government to a pond where big fish eat the small fish.
(a) According to the chapter, why did Washington refuse?
(b) What does Kautilya's picture say a government must ensure, and what must the king follow?
(c) Which feature of a republic does Washington's choice show?
(d) Which story shows the need for a government and which the need for limits on a ruler? Using both, say whether the motion can be supported without ignoring one of them.
questions.a: (a) He believed only in a government by the people under a constitution and thought a king would harm the country. (b) Law and order; the king must follow Raja Dharma. (c) A republic limits the ruler's power by a constitution or laws and has no hereditary king. (d) Kautilya's story shows the need for a government; Washington's shows the need for limits on a ruler. The motion cannot be supported without ignoring the limits: even Kautilya's king follows Raja Dharma, so a strong ruler without limits is not what either story praises.
s: Part (a): he believed only in government by the people under a constitution
Part (b): law and order, and the king follows Raja Dharma
Part (c): limits on a ruler through a constitution or laws, no hereditary king
Part (d): matches each story to its lesson and shows the motion ignores the limits

questions.q: For how long do members of the political executive usually stay in power, unless they are re-elected or dismissed?

questions.q: (a) Give two examples of grassroots bureaucrats listed in the chapter. (b) Why does the chapter say our interactions are usually with them?

questions.q: (a) How long does the political executive usually stay in power? (b) On what does its power depend, and how is that different for the permanent executive?
questions.a: (a) Usually five years. (b) Its power depends on the trust and support of the people. The permanent executive is selected through examinations, not elected, and is not replaced after every election.

questions.q: What does the legislature do in a democracy, and why does the chapter say governance happens through laws and not personal wishes?
questions.a: It represents the people and makes laws that apply to everyone. Governance by well-defined laws avoids arbitrary decisions based on personal wishes.
s: Makes laws for everyone, representing the people
Laws rather than personal wishes or arbitrary decisions

questions.q: Name two large programmes managed by the bureaucracy, from the chapter's list, and say why they need a body of officers that does not change with every election.

questions.q: What undertaking were women in the Indian Foreign Service made to sign, as C.B. Muthamma recalled, and which court later struck down such gender-biased provisions?

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Ministers and civil servants do the same job, so a government needs only one of them.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter.

questions.a: The political executive consists of elected leaders such as the prime minister, chief ministers and ministers, with the president and governors mostly formal. They are elected, stay for a fixed time, usually five years, and make big decisions, introduce laws, set goals and represent India abroad. The permanent executive consists of officers selected through examinations like the UPSC's, who are not replaced after elections and give expert advice, implement policies and manage services. Both are needed because the elected leaders reflect people's trust and set directions while the officers keep government running smoothly whichever party is in power.

questions.q: Some years ago a government department made women officers of the Indian Foreign Service sign an undertaking to resign if they married. A senior woman officer, denied promotion, went to the Supreme Court, which struck down such gender-biased provisions as violating the Constitution. questions.a: The claim is wrong. The department belongs to the executive, whose officers carry out and administer the government's work, but it is not above the Constitution. The Supreme Court struck down the undertaking as violating the Constitution, so a department's rule is valid only if it follows the Constitution. The case shows that even permanent-executive rules can be corrected, that elected leaders and officers alike are bound by the law, and that the pursuit of gender equality in public service was advanced by a citizen using the courts.

Links to the idea that the executive too is bound by the Constitution and the law
Judges the claim wrong with a reasoned verdict about gender equality in public service

questions.q:
After floods, 2,400 families in 12 villages of Raigad district are to get relief. The state's ministers announce that all 2,400 families will be verified within 6 days. The district's officers form 8 verification teams. Each team can verify 25 families a day.
(a) Which executive took the decision to give relief, and which will carry it out?
(b) How many days will the 8 teams need to verify all the families, and which key function of the bureaucracy is being measured?
(c) How many teams are needed to keep the 6-day promise?
(d) If the promise is broken, who must answer to the people, the ministers or the officers, and why?
questions.a: (a) The political executive decides; the permanent executive carries it out. (b) 2,400 / (8 x 25) = 12 days; implementing laws, policies and schemes. (c) 2,400 / (25 x 6) = 16 teams, that is 8 more than now. (d) The ministers, because the political executive is elected and its power depends on the trust and support of the people; the officers are selected through examinations, not elected, and carry on whichever party is in power.
s: Part (a): political executive decides, permanent executive carries out
Part (b): 12 days and implementing schemes
Part (c): 16 teams
Part (d): the ministers, because their power depends on people's trust

questions.q:

(c) Whom would villagers meet most often, and what does the chapter call such officials?

questions.a: (a) The minister is the political executive; the other three are the permanent executive. (b) The minister's post depends on the election; the three officers are not removed or replaced after every election. (c) The village health worker; a grassroots bureaucrat. (d) A permanent-executive guest, best the district health officer or the village health worker, because the minister decides the goal and the scheme but officers deliver it in the village; choosing the minister is the weaker answer for the question asked, although the minister can explain why the scheme was started.
s: Part (a): minister political, the other three permanent
Part (b): minister's post depends on the election, the others continue
Part (c): village health worker, a grassroots bureaucrat
Part (d): chooses an officer or health worker because delivery is done by the permanent executive

Transparency and accountability

questions.a: The government is protector (law and defence, e.g. police forces), provider (public welfare and infrastructure, e.g. free schools, roads and railways) and regulator (of economic activity and social justice, e.g. food safety). In the second, a plan would fill a large lake with construction waste. For each problem choose the most suitable route from the chapter and justify it, and say what each route needs to succeed.
questions.a: For the road, the Right to Information Act: officials are bound to give the information on how the money was spent, which brings transparency and accountability, and with those facts residents can press the officials to repair the work. questions.q:

(b) Under which of the government's three roles does building roads fall?
(c) What percent of households support the RTI, to the nearest whole number, and what does the chapter's idea of accountability then require of the officials?
(d) Is the secretary right that the RTI is a waste of time? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) The money spent on the road repair; transparency and accountability. (b) The provider role (infrastructure such as roads). (c) 95/150 = 63 percent; those in power must answer for their actions to the public. (d) No. The potholes show that the work is poor but not how the ₹18 lakh was spent; only the RTI gives that, and with facts the residents can hold the officials accountable. The post can be used along with it to draw attention.
s: Part (a): spending on the road; transparency and accountability
Part (b): provider role
Part (c): 63 percent and officials must answer to the public
Part (d): No, because the RTI gives the facts of spending that potholes do not

questions.q:
Mahi's project on the Silent Valley has a timeline: 1970, the Kerala Government plans a hydroelectric project that would have submerged vast tracts of evergreen forest; 1983, the project is cancelled; 1985, the valley becomes a National Park. questions.a: (a) The Central Government cancelled it; non-government organisations led the opposition. (b) Scientists, environmentalists, writers, public figures, teachers and local villagers. (c) Option (ii), forming an NGO and mobilising public opinion. (d) Option (i) or (iii) first, because the NGO campaign took 13 years (1970 to 1983) in Silent Valley and the lake would be gone before then; the portal promises a response in a specified time. The residents can start the NGO campaign along with it for lasting protection.
s: Part (a): the Central Government; NGOs led the opposition
Part (b): scientists, writers, teachers, villagers and others
Part (c): option (ii), NGO and public opinion
Part (d): a quick route first, using the 13 years the campaign took

It interprets laws when their wording is complex or people disagree on the meaning
It settles disputes and protects people's rights
It checks whether laws made by the government are fair and just

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of the judiciary's work and not of the executive's?
questions.a: Judicial review, setting aside a law that violates the Constitution, is the judiciary's work. Checking that schools follow a law, investigating and announcing schemes belong to the executive.
o: A court declares a state law invalid because it violates the Constitution
A Block Education Officer checks that schools follow a law on toilets
The police investigate a theft
A minister announces a new scheme

questions.q: Two neighbours in a Madurai colony read the same sentence of a law differently. One thinks a shop may stay open till 11 pm, the other thinks till 9 pm. They take the matter to a court. Which function of the judiciary is at work?
questions.a: When the wording of a law is complex or people disagree on its meaning, the judiciary interprets the law and explains what it means.
o: Interpreting the law
Safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review
Making a new law for the colony
Enforcing the law by sending officers to the shop

questions.q: A state law bans a community from practising its religion. A citizen goes to the High Court, which declares the law invalid because it violates the Constitution. Which function of the judiciary is most directly shown by the court declaring the law invalid?
questions.a: Checking whether a law follows the Constitution and setting it aside if it does not is safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review.
o: Safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review
Interpreting a law whose wording is complex
Investigating a crime and presenting the case to court
Making a new law to replace the old one

questions.q:
Read the following statements.
1. The judiciary works under the control of the government of the day so that justice is quick.
2. The judiciary makes laws for the country and for each state.
3. The judiciary protects the rule of law, so everyone, even the government, must follow the law.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 3 is correct. The judiciary is independent and not controlled by the government, and it is the legislature that makes laws.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Courts interpret laws when their wording is complex or people disagree on their meaning.
Reason (R): The judiciary in India is independent and not controlled by the government or politicians.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Courts interpret laws because wording can be complex or disputed; independence is a separate feature that keeps justice fair and equal.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name any three things the chapter says the judiciary does. (b) Which one would a citizen use when her fundamental rights are violated?
questions.a: (a) Any three of: protects and defends the laws, interprets the laws, protects the rights and liberty of citizens, safeguards the Constitution through judicial review. (b) Protecting rights and liberty: she can go to court to address the violation.
s: Part (a): three correct functions
Part (b): protects rights and liberty, by going to court

questions.q: (a) What is the rule of law? (b) Why does the chapter say the judiciary is needed to protect it?
questions.a: (a) The idea that everyone must follow the law, even the government. (b) The judiciary keeps a check on unfair actions, ensures that laws do not harm people's rights and resolves conflicts peacefully.
s: Part (a): everyone, even the government, must follow the law
Part (b): checks unfair actions, protects rights, resolves conflicts peacefully

questions.q: Why is a referee a suitable comparison for the judiciary acting through judicial review?
questions.a: A referee decides who has broken the rules and is not on one side of the game. The judiciary acts as a referee when the government or others break the law, so it must be fair and independent of them.
s: A referee judges who breaks the rules in a game, as the judiciary does when the law is broken (credit as application of the comparison)
Neither is on one side, so the judiciary must be independent of the government

questions.q: What does it mean to say the judiciary is independent? Give one benefit the chapter mentions.
questions.a: It is not controlled by the government or politicians. This helps keep justice fair and equal for all.
s: Not controlled by the government or politicians
Benefit: justice is fair and equal for all

questions.q: A court sets aside an order by which a government office unfairly cancelled a widow's licence. Which benefit of a judiciary that protects the rule of law from the chapter does this show, and what is one other benefit it lists?
questions.a: It shows that the judiciary keeps a check on unfair actions. Another benefit is that it ensures laws do not harm people's rights, or that it resolves conflicts peacefully.
s: Check on unfair actions
One other benefit from the chapter

questions.q: Neha says, 'A court can protect our rights only if the government agrees to it.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The judiciary is independent and not controlled by the government or politicians. If fundamental rights are violated, we can go to court, and the judiciary checks whether laws made by the government are fair and just. Everyone, even the government, must follow the law.
s: Verdict: disagrees
The judiciary is independent of the government
Citizens can go to court and the government too must follow the law

questions.q: Show that a judiciary controlled by the government could not act as a referee between the government and a citizen.
questions.a: A referee has to be independent of the players. If the government controlled the judiciary, the judge would be on one side when the government broke the law. It could not keep a check on unfair actions and justice would not be fair and equal for all.
s: A referee must not belong to one side
A controlled judiciary would be on the government's side when the government breaks the law
So it could not check unfair actions or keep justice fair and equal

questions.q: Explain 'interprets the laws' and 'protects the rights and liberty of citizens', giving one example of your own for each.
questions.a: Interpreting: explaining what a law means when the wording is complex or people disagree, e.g. what 'public place' means in a rule. Protecting rights: citizens can go to court if fundamental rights are violated, e.g. a person denied equal treatment goes to court.
s: Meaning of interprets the laws
Meaning of protecting rights, going to court
A suitable example for each

questions.q: Read three news items. (1) A court explains what 'public place' means in a rule, as two groups read it differently. (2) A court orders a government office to restore a family's ration card, saying their rights were violated. (3) A High Court declares a section of a state law invalid because it violates the Constitution. Name the function of the judiciary shown in each, explain why the third makes the judiciary the 'guardian of the Constitution', and say what citizens would lose if the court could do only the first two.
questions.a: (1) Interpreting the laws. (2) Protecting the rights and liberty of citizens. (3) Safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review. In (3) the court checks whether a law made by the government follows the Constitution and sets it aside if it does not, acting as a referee when the government breaks the law; this is why it is the guardian of the Constitution. If it could do only the first two, citizens would have no check on laws that harm their rights, since the government's own laws would stand unquestioned.
s: Item 1: interpreting the laws
Item 2: protecting rights and liberty of citizens
Item 3: safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review
Why this makes the judiciary the guardian of the Constitution
What citizens would lose: no check on laws that harm rights

questions.q: Imagine a country in which the government can dismiss any judge who rules against it. Using the chapter, analyse what would happen to (i) a citizen whose rights are violated, (ii) a law that harms people's rights, and (iii) a dispute between a citizen and the government. Conclude whether such a country can keep the rule of law.
questions.a: (i) The citizen could not rely on going to court, since judges would fear dismissal, so her rights would not be protected. (ii) No one could check whether a government law is fair and just, because judicial review needs an independent judiciary. (iii) The government would be on both sides of the dispute, so a referee would be missing and justice would not be fair or equal. The rule of law, that everyone including the government must follow the law, could not be kept.
s: (i) Citizen's rights would not be protected
(ii) No check on laws that harm rights, so no judicial review
(iii) No independent referee in a dispute with the government
Links each to the loss of fair and equal justice
Concludes the rule of law could not be kept

questions.q:
On one Monday three matters come up in the courts. In the first, in a district court, two farmers disagree about what a state law on sharing canal water means for their village. In the second, in a district court, a woman says a private company's rule denies promotion to married women, and she cites the Constitution. In the third, in a High Court, a citizens' group says a new state law goes against the Constitution. In all three matters the government of the state accepts and follows the court's orders.
(a) Name the function of the judiciary that each of the three matters shows.
(b) In the third matter, why must the court be independent of the government that made the law?
(c) What does the government's acceptance of the orders show about the rule of law?
(d) A minister suggests a committee of ministers should approve every verdict before it is announced, to avoid mistakes and delays. Should this be accepted? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) First: interpreting the law. Second: protecting citizens' rights. Third: safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review. (b) It must check whether a law made by the government is fair and just, which it cannot do if the government controls it. (c) Everyone, even the government, must follow the law. (d) Reject it: approval would end independence and the court could no longer check the government; the only argument for accepting it is speed and caution, which does not outweigh fair and equal justice.
s: Part (a): interprets, protects rights, judicial review
Part (b): it must check a law of the government, so it cannot be controlled by it
Part (c): the government too must follow the law
Part (d): a clear decision weighing mistakes and delays against independence

questions.q:
A department of a state government begins building a new office on a plot without following the legal process to obtain it. The plot's owners, a family in a small town, go to court. The court hears both sides, finds the construction unlawful and orders it to stop. A minister says, 'The court is blocking development, and the department should carry on.' A villager replies, 'The law applies to the government too.'
(a) Which idea does the villager state, and what is the chapter's name for it?
(b) On what ground could the family go to court?
(c) What feature of the judiciary allowed it to rule against a government department?
(d) Should the department carry on as the minister says? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) The rule of law. (b) That the legal process for acquiring the land was not followed; the rule of law applies to the government too, so the family may ask the court to check the unfair action. (c) Its independence from the government and politicians. (d) No. The department must obey the order because the rule of law applies to the government; it can restart the work only by following the legal process properly or by choosing another plot.
s: Part (a): the rule of law, that everyone including the government must follow the law
Part (b): the legal process for acquiring the land was not followed
Part (c): independence from the government
Part (d): No, because the rule of law binds the government

questions.q: Which of the following is among the matters the chapter assigns to local governments?
questions.a: Local governments work in villages, towns and cities to solve local problems such as water, drainage, streetlamps and parks. Defence, foreign affairs and currency belong to the Union Government.
o: Drainage and streetlamps
Currency and foreign affairs
Defence of the country
Marriage laws for the whole country

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT given in the chapter as a benefit of decentralisation?
questions.a: The chapter lists stronger local governments, better local knowledge, more democracy, local discussions and more accountability. A single office taking every decision is the opposite of decentralisation.
o: A single office can take every decision faster
Stronger local governments with real power
Better knowledge of the local area and its needs
More accountability of leaders to the people

questions.q: How many states and union territories does India have, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says India, as a federal country, has 28 states and 8 union territories.
o: 28 states and 8 union territories
28 states and 7 union territories
29 states and 7 union territories
8 states and 28 union territories

questions.q: The Union Government in Delhi decides the exact position of every streetlamp in thousands of villages. Meera says, 'This will go wrong.' Which idea from the chapter supports her?
questions.a: The chapter says local problems should be solved locally because local leaders know the area and its needs better than distant officials, while bigger issues go to higher governments.
o: Local leaders know the area better, so local problems are solved locally
Bigger issues go to higher levels, so Delhi alone should decide all matters
Streetlamps are a concurrent subject, so only the Union can decide them
Only the courts can decide on the position of streetlamps

questions.q: A state legislature passes a law that every school must have separate toilets for girls and boys. A Block Education Officer visits schools to see that this is done, and the State Council for the Protection of Child Rights acts when a school ignores a girl's right. Which option names the roles correctly?
questions.a: The legislature makes the law, the permanent executive (the Block Education Officer) ensures that it is followed, and a body such as the SCPCR protects children's rights.
o: Legislature makes the law; the Block Education Officer implements it; the SCPCR protects rights
Executive makes the law; the legislature implements it; the SCPCR protects rights
Legislature makes the law; the SCPCR implements it; the Block Education Officer protects rights
Judiciary makes the law; the Block Education Officer protects rights; the SCPCR approves budgets

questions.q:
Read the following statements.
1. When the Constitution first came into force, local governments were already a separate third tier.
2. Decentralisation means that power and decision-making are spread out and not concentrated in one place or one small group.
3. Gandhi's idea of village swaraj was a village completely independent of every other village in all its needs.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 2 is correct. Local governments were not separate levels originally and were listed under the State List. Gandhi described a village independent for its vital wants and yet interdependent for many others.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Local governments are called the third tier of India's democracy.
Reason (R): The original Constitution provided for panchayats and municipalities as separate constitutional levels.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Originally there were only two levels and local governments were listed under the State List; they became the third tier through an amendment in the early 1990s.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with the body that handles it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Defence and currency  2. Police and health within a state  3. Drainage and streetlamps  4. Acting when a school ignores a girl's right to education
Column B: a. local governments  b. state governments  c. Union Government  d. the State Council for the Protection of Child Rights
questions.a: Defence and currency are Union matters, police and health in a state are state matters, drainage and streetlamps are local, and acting when a school ignores a girl's right is the work of a rights body such as the SCPCR. The wrong pairings swap the Union with the states or the local level with the rights body.

questions.q: (a) How many levels of government did the Constitution originally provide for, and where did panchayats and municipalities stand? (b) What was the aim of the change made in the early 1990s?
questions.a: (a) Two levels, the Union and the states; local governments were not separate levels and were listed under the State List, so state governments decided how they worked. (b) To strengthen democracy at the grassroots and enable people to participate directly in decision-making.
s: Part (a): two levels; local governments under the State List
Part (b): strengthen grassroots democracy and direct participation

questions.q: (a) State in one line the idea behind decentralisation. (b) Using it, say who should deal with a damaged village road and who with the country's defence.
questions.a: (a) Power and decision-making are spread out, local problems are solved locally and bigger issues by higher-level governments. (b) The local government (panchayat) for the road and the Central Government for defence.
s: Part (a): power spread out, local problems solved locally, bigger issues by higher levels
Part (b): local government for the road, Central Government for defence

questions.q: Give any two reasons from the chapter why decisions on local matters should be taken locally.
questions.a: Local leaders know the area, its needs and traditions better than distant officials; people are more involved in decisions that affect daily life; local issues can be discussed by people who face them every day; it is easier to question leaders who are close to the people.
s: First reason
Second reason

questions.q: Why does the chapter say that a single central government cannot meet the needs of all of India's people? Give two points.
questions.a: India has over 1.4 billion people and thousands of towns and villages, and it has 28 states and 8 union territories. It also has many languages and cultures, so governance has to be decentralised at multiple levels.
s: Size: over 1.4 billion people, thousands of towns and villages, 28 states and 8 union territories
Diversity of languages and cultures, so decentralised governance

questions.q: Which tier of government (Union, state or local) handles each of these: (i) designing and printing rupee notes, (ii) streetlamps on a road in Nashik, (iii) the police force of Maharashtra? Give the chapter's reason for any one of your answers.
questions.a: (i) Union Government, (ii) local government, (iii) state government. Reason, for example: local problems such as streetlamps are solved locally because local leaders know the area and its needs better; currency is a matter for the whole country, so it stays with the Union Government.
s: All three tiers matched correctly
A reason from the chapter for one answer

questions.q: Kabir says, 'If power is shared with panchayats and municipalities, the Union Government becomes weak and cannot defend the country.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. Decentralisation spreads out decision-making, with local problems solved locally and bigger issues by higher governments. Defence, foreign affairs and currency remain with the Central Government, so sharing power for local matters does not take over its work.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Local matters go to local governments and bigger issues to higher governments
Defence and other national matters stay with the Union Government

questions.q: Show that a country could not leave defence and currency to each local government separately.
questions.a: The chapter says bigger issues are decided by higher-level governments and local problems by local ones. Defence, foreign affairs and currency concern the whole country and are Union subjects. If thousands of village and city bodies each decided them, there would be thousands of different policies and currencies and the country could not be defended or its money used everywhere, so such matters must stay with the Union Government.
s: Bigger issues go to higher-level governments
Defence and currency are Union matters concerning the whole country
Separate decisions by thousands of local bodies would give conflicting policies, so they cannot be local

questions.q: Explain Gandhi's idea of village swaraj and say how it is connected to decentralisation.
questions.a: Gandhi strongly supported largely self-sufficient village governments called gram swaraj, a complete republic, independent of its neighbours for its own vital wants and yet interdependent for many others. This is decentralisation: power rests with the village.
s: Gram swaraj: self-sufficient village government
Independent for vital wants yet interdependent for many others
Link to decentralisation, power with local people

questions.q: A village school's girls' toilets exist only on paper, although a state law requires them. Using the chapter's school-education example, trace how the legislature, the permanent executive, the political executive and the judiciary or a child rights body could each help set this right.
questions.a: The legislature has already made the law that schools must have separate toilets for girls and boys. The permanent executive, officers such as the District and Block Education Officers, ensures that laws are followed and can inspect and act. The political executive, ministers at union and state levels, guides policy and makes rules and can provide schemes and funds. The judiciary, courts and bodies like the NCPCR and SCPCR, protects children's rights and can act if a school ignores a girl's right. Union and state levels both play a part.
s: Legislature made the law requiring the toilets
Permanent executive ensures the law is followed
Political executive guides policy and makes rules or schemes
Judiciary or child rights bodies protect the girl's right
Notes the union and state levels both play a part

questions.q: 'Local problems should be solved locally, and bigger issues by higher-level governments.' Justify this principle using the tasks of the three tiers and the reasons for decentralisation, and say why local governments became the third tier.
questions.a: The Union Government looks after the whole country, such as defence, foreign affairs and currency. State governments handle needs of each state, like police, land, health and agriculture. Local governments handle water, drainage, streetlamps and parks. Local decisions are made where leaders know the area better, people take part more, local issues are discussed by those who face them and leaders are easier to question. In the early 1990s an amendment made panchayats and municipalities the third tier to strengthen democracy at the grassroots.
s: Union tasks with examples
State tasks with examples
Local tasks with examples
Reasons for deciding locally
Early 1990s amendment creating the third tier to strengthen grassroots democracy

questions.q:
A Class 7 'Mini-India' project in Coimbatore gives the class eight tasks to sort among the three tiers: defence, streetlamps, state police, drainage, currency, parks, health services of the state, and foreign affairs. The ward councillor of the real city then proposes that streetlamps and parks, now handled by the local body, should move to the state government, because buying lamps and park equipment in bulk would cut costs.
(a) Sort the eight tasks among the Union, state and local governments, and say what percent of the eight go to the local tier.
(b) Name two benefits of decentralisation that the councillor's proposal would weaken.
(c) Why does the saving from bulk buying not settle the question, according to the chapter's principle for local matters?
(d) Should the proposal be accepted? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Union: defence, currency, foreign affairs. State: state police and health services. Local: streetlamps, drainage, parks; 3/8 = 37.5 percent. (b) Any two of better local knowledge, more accountability, local discussion, more democracy. (c) The chapter says local problems should be solved locally by leaders who know the area, so cost alone does not decide. (d) No. Moving streetlamps and parks to the state loses local knowledge and the ease of questioning leaders; the saving can be pursued by the local body, for example by buying together with other local bodies.
s: Part (a): correct sorting and 37.5 percent local
Part (b): two benefits of decentralisation named
Part (c): local problems are solved locally by leaders who know the area
Part (d): No, justified with the lost benefits

questions.q:
The villagers of a gram panchayat in Telangana send a petition with five demands: (1) repair the drinking-water pipeline, (2) clear the village drains, (3) change the design of rupee coins, (4) post a police constable in the village, (5) change the country's policy on a treaty with another country. The sarpanch says, 'Let us send all five to Delhi, since Delhi has the most money and the most power.'
(a) Which of the five demands can the panchayat itself handle, and to which tier does each of the others belong?
(b) Give one reason from the chapter why the pipeline and drains are better decided locally.
(c) What percent of the five demands belong to the Union Government?
(d) Is the sarpanch right to send all five to Delhi? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) The panchayat can handle (1) and (2). Demand (3) is the Union Government's (currency), (4) is the state government's (police), and (5) is the Union Government's (foreign affairs). (b) Local leaders know the area and its needs better, and it is easier to question leaders who are close to the people. (c) 2 of 5 = 40 percent. (d) No. Local problems such as water and drainage are to be solved locally; sending them to Delhi loses local knowledge and accountability. Only demand (3) and (5) go to the Union, and (4) to the state.
s: Part (a): demands 1 and 2 local, 3 and 5 Union, 4 state
Part (b): local knowledge or ease of questioning leaders
Part (c): 40 percent
Part (d): No, local problems are solved locally; others go to their own tiers
